title: India’s Nutrition Paradox: Why Are We Eating More but Nourishing Less?

contentHtml:
Walk through any Indian city today and the food story looks like one of abundance. Delivery apps reach every lane, supermarket shelves overflow, and festive tables groan. Yet in my clinical practice, the patients who sit across from me, whether they are a young professional with fatty liver, a new mother with severe fatigue or a child who is overweight but anaemic, tell a different story. We are eating more than ever but we are not nourishing ourselves better.

This is India's nutrition paradox, and it is one of the most important public health challenges of time.Two burdens, one plate: For decades, India's nutrition challenge meant undernutrition: stunting, wasting and underweight children. That problem has not gone away. National Family Health Survey data show that more than a third of children under five are stunted, and over half of women of reproductive age are anaemic.

Advt

At the same time, a second burden has risen alongside it. Overweight and obesity are climbing across age groups. India is home to over 100 million people with diabetes and an even larger group with prediabetes, according to the ICMR-INDIAB study. Hypertension, fatty liver disease and dyslipidaemia now appear in people in their twenties and thirties.

What makes this a paradox is that these conditions often coexist, sometimes in the same household and sometimes in the same person. A person can carry excess weight and still be deficient in iron, vitamin B12, vitamin D, folate and calcium. "Hidden hunger": the body is fed enough energy but starved of the micronutrients it needs to function.

Calories are not the same as nutrition: The root of the problem is simple. Energy and nourishment are not the same thing.

Over the past two decades, the Indian diet has shifted. Refined cereals, polished rice and maida have gradually displaced millets, pulses and whole grains. Packaged snacks, sugar-sweetened beverages, instant noodles, biscuits and fried convenience foods have become everyday staples rather than occasional treats. These ultra-processed foods are calorie-dense, easy to overeat and low in fibre, protein, vitamins and minerals.

The traditional Indian plate was, in many ways, nutritionally wise. A balanced thali combined cereal, dal, vegetables, curd, a little fat and seasonal produce. Today that structure is eroding. Meals are skipped, vegetables are the first thing to be cut from a rushed lunch, and protein is often an afterthought. A breakfast of tea and a biscuit, a lunch of rice with a thin dal only and an evening of namkeen and chai can add up to plenty of calories and very little nutrition.

Advt

Why Indians face a particular risk:Body composition: Indians tend to develop more abdominal and visceral fat at lower body weights than many other populations. A person with a "normal" BMI can still carry metabolic risk. This is often described as the "thin-fat" phenotype.Low protein quality and quantity: Our diets are heavily cereal-based. Many people, vegetarians in particular, do not get adequate protein, and this affects muscle mass, immunity, satiety and recovery.Micronutrient gaps: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread despite abundant sunshine, because of indoor lifestyles and covered clothing. Vitamin B12 and Iron deficiency persists across income groups.

Advt

Sedentary living: Desk-bound work, long commutes and screen time mean we burn less while the food environment pushes us to consume more.It is not only a poverty story: One of the most common misconceptions is that poor nutrition is only a problem of low income. It is not. Affluent households often have excellent access to food but poor food choices, driven by convenience, aggressive marketing, irregular meal timings and limited nutrition literacy. In lower-income households, the challenge is access to diverse, affordable and nutrient-rich foods. Both groups are vulnerable, for different reasons.

Nutrition literacy is the thread that connects them. Many people can read a calorie count, but far fewer understand fibre, protein quality, added sugar or what a balanced plate looks like. "Low fat" or "high protein" labels are often mistaken for guarantees of health.What the early years teach us: Nutrition is not a problem we can fix in adulthood alone. The first 1,000 days, from conception to a child's second birthday, shape lifelong metabolic health, brain development and immunity. Maternal nutrition, breastfeeding, appropriate complementary foods and early food habits matter enormously. A child who is undernourished early and then exposed to calorie-rich, nutrient-poor food later is at heightened risk of obesity and diabetes in adulthood.Practical shifts that make a difference: The good news is that the solutions are neither exotic nor expensive. Much of the answer lies in returning to what our food culture already knew.

  • Rebuild the balanced plate: Aim for half the plate as vegetables and salads, a quarter for protein (dal, legumes, eggs, fish, paneer, curd, chicken) and a quarter for whole grains.
  • Bring back millets and whole grains: Ragi, jowar and bajra, along with unpolished rice and whole wheat, offer more fibre and micronutrients than refined alternatives.
  • Eat protein at all meals: Consuming protein at all meals helps with muscle, satiety and blood glucose management.
  • Treat packaged foods as occasional, not daily: Reading labels for added sugar, sodium and refined flour helps, but fresh, minimally processed food is the best default.
  • Eat the seasonal rainbow: Varied colours on the plate usually mean varied vitamins, minerals and antioxidants.
  • Get screened: Periodic checks for haemoglobin, vitamin D, B12 and blood sugar can catch deficiencies and metabolic risk long before symptoms appear.
  • Move daily: Nutrition and physical activity work together. Neither can fully compensate for the absence of the other.

Nutrition is clinical care: Nutrition should not be treated as an afterthought in healthcare. It is central to prevention, recovery, management of chronic disease and healthy ageing. Nutrition assessment and intervention within a clinical setting can promote recovery and reduce risks. Failure to address malnutrition may result in increased burden and costs.A shared responsibility: Individual decisions count, yet they are influenced by the environment surrounding us. Real change will need families, schools, workplaces, food manufacturers, healthcare professionals and policymakers working in the same direction: clearer labelling, healthier options in canteens and public institutions, stronger nutrition education in schools, and wider access to qualified dietetic guidance.India does not have a food shortage problem alone, nor a food excess problem alone. It has a food quality problem. The measure of a healthy nation is not how much its people eat but how well that food nourishes them.If we want a population that is productive, resilient and free of avoidable disease, the question to ask at every meal is no longer "Have I eaten enough?" but "Has this meal nourished me?"This article is written by Dr Eileen Canday, Head of Department of Nutrition & Dietetics, Sir H.N Reliance Foundation Hospital.(DISCLAIMER: The views expressed are solely of the author and ETHealthworld.com does not necessarily subscribe to it.
